title: Private Deployments risk heatmap and decision guidance
content:
Purpose:
This brief is a compact decision aid for field sellers and SEs to evaluate buyer maturity, map risks, and choose the fastest path to a closed pilot for regulated workloads. It focuses on control-plane language that reduces legal/friction while preserving Redwood's product guarantees.

Executive summary (two sentences):
Regulated buyers want assurance that their data, keys, and auditables remain under their control while still benefiting from Redwood's managed upgrades, fallbacks, and performance guarantees. Positioning the control plane as a thin coordination layer (customer-owned telemetry, configurable sync windows, and explicit admin consent for schema/ops) preserves trust while keeping the integration lift low.

Buyer persona heatmap (quick view):
- CISO / Security Leadership: Risk tolerance low, auditability high. Primary asks: key custody, incident response, proof of isolation, regulatory evidence.
- CTO / Platform: Operational continuity, deployment templates, observability of SLOs, predictable cost.
- Procurement / Legal: Licensing model, indemnity, data residency clauses, SLAs and exit terms.
- App/Product PM: Time-to-market, easy SDKs, predictable latency and costs.

Risk vector matrix (interpretable guidance for reps):
- Data residency: High risk. Recommended controls: VPC-only egress rules, regional hosting, explicit data residency clause in SOW.
- Control plane telemetry: Medium risk if opaque. Recommended controls: provide telemetry schema, sampling controls, hashed identifiers (never PII), option for no telemetry (audit-only mode).
- Key management: Critical. Recommended controls: customer-managed KMS + HSM option, signed attestations for key rotation events, short path to key revocation and wipe.
- Software updates: Medium risk for regulated buyers. Recommended controls: scheduled maintenance windows, optional manual approval for major agent upgrades, rollback guarantees and snapshots.
- Incident provenance & audit: Critical. Recommended controls: immutable audit logs delivered to buyer-owned storage, runbooks sharing, SOC2/ISO artifacts, optional e-Discovery exports.

Control plane language — concise phrasings for field use:
- Neutral, non-technical framing: "Redwood provides a coordination layer that orchestrates model routing and capacity. You keep ownership of keys, telemetry, and audit trails — Redwood only stores lightweight control metadata unless you opt-in otherwise."
- For CISOs: "Control plane operations are governed by customer consent gates. We support customer-managed KMS and direct-delivery audit logs to your S3/GCS buckets."
- For Architects: "Think of the control plane as a control channel, not a data path: inference inputs and outputs can remain entirely in your VPC — the control plane orchestrates model versioning, routing policies, and metrics collection on your terms."

Common buyer objections + pragmatic rebuttals (short scripts):
1) Objection: "We can't allow any vendor control plane—our compliance forbids external orchestration."
   Rebuttal: "Understood. We offer a private control plane deployment option that runs inside your VPC or on-prem. For many pilots we start with a dedicated control-plane image that you host; telemetry can be delivered to your storage and our operators only have read-access via an auditable process."
2) Objection: "If we hand over keys or telemetry, we lose control."
   Rebuttal: "You don't hand them over. Key material stays in your KMS/HSM; Redwood receives short-lived attestations for operations. Telemetry schema and sampling are configurable and can be hashed or anonymized by default."
3) Objection: "We need legal indemnity for model outputs in regulated contexts."
   Rebuttal: "We'll scope the pilot to a bounded workload and include output-review gates and rollback triggers. For enterprise contracts we provide tailored indemnity language and operational SLAs — we'll loop Legal early to align the SOW."

Competitive differentiation framing (talking points vs two archetypes):
- Versus "Cloud vendor managed endpoints": emphasize predictable unit economics and fine-grained control over inference routing and quantization. Cloud-managed endpoints may accept data into their control planes by default; we emphasize optional telemetry and customer-hosted control plane variants.
- Versus "Self-hosted inference open-source stacks": emphasize we provide production-grade operational tooling (autoscaling, KV caching, fallback policies) and an ops playbook so customers don't reallocate platform engineers to babysit inference clusters.

Pilot design patterns that reduce procurement friction:
- Single-service pilot: deploy Redwood private control-plane image into a test VPC, restrict external egress, validate telemetry export, run a 30-day workload with 3-4 production-simulated routes. Success metrics: <100ms p50 inference, audit logs delivered within SLA, zero keys exported.
- Air-gapped validation (for very regulated pilots): provide a signed bundle and runbook, on-site SE-assisted install, weekly checkpoint exports of audit logs and performance traces. Success metrics: install checklist complete, replayed inference traces validate parity.

Pricing anchors & commercial levers (field guidance):
- Start with a predictable reserved-capacity SKU for pilot (monthly minimum) that includes 24/7 onboarding support and audit artifact delivery.
- Offer a limited-time waiver for professional services hours to cover KMS/HSM integration and runbook tailoring.
- Use a two-stage commercial path: pilot -> validated pilot (SLA + compliance evidence) -> commit (annual reserved capacity + extended support).

Negotiation play (what to concede and what to hold):
- Concede early: limited telemetry subset, temporary access windows for debugging, first-month PS hours. These reduce friction without exposing long-term risk.
- Hold firm: customer-managed key exclusivity, permanent audit export granting, and formal exit/export clauses.

Artifacts to attach in the sales cycle (recommended):
- Short technical appendix describing KMS/HSM integration steps (deliverable).
- Checklist for in-VPC control-plane deployment and required firewall rules.
- A compliance package with SOC2 report, ISO artifacts, and a short traceability matrix mapping product controls to common frameworks.

Open questions for product/legal before wide rollout:
- Can we produce a short, redacted attestation template that demonstrates "no sensitive telemetry retained" for buyers who need audit proof?
- What is the fastest path to provide an immutable, customer-delivered audit log export with retention controls that match buyer policies?
- Are we willing to codify a standard template of indemnity for regulated model outputs or do we prefer case-by-case legal review?

Suggested next steps for GTM:
- Quick wins (1–2 weeks): create the KMS integration appendix and a one-page control-plane privacy fact sheet for SEs and AEs.
- Medium (3–6 weeks): build out the pilot playbook (templates for SOW, runbook, install checklist) and a short demo script for air-gapped installs.
- Longer (quarter roadmap): enable an audit-export UI that pushes to customer buckets and an opt-in "minimal telemetry" mode to reduce initial friction.

Appendix: sample email subject lines and opening sentences for outreach
- Subject: "Quick question about control-plane options for secure LLM inference"
- Body first line: "We can run Redwood's control plane entirely in your VPC and deliver audit logs directly to your storage — would you be open to a 30-day technical pilot scoped to a small regulated workload?"

Short sign-off (for SEs):
Keep the framing simple: control plane = coordination, not data custody. Start pilots small, make telemetry explicit and reversible, and escalate legal templates early. This approach preserves buyer trust while keeping integration timelines short.
